Senses.Explanation: One can know propriety is a line from a traditional primer sequence that Chan speakers quote, splice, and deploy as an interview reply or learned-speech cap. Its literal claim concerns recognizing proper conduct; its corpus job comes from the exact exchange or recitation around it. Jianfu Chenggu performs a mock qin gesture and recites the primer chain through 'one can know propriety.' Chushi Fanqi inserts the phrase between the two halves of Shakyamuni's birth declaration. Jinian Jingxian glosses a verse line by line with the primer and ends on the phrase. Dahui Zonggao recites it after classical and primer lines, then asks how Baofeng compares with Confucius and caps the address with a line about speaking poetry to one who understands. These are observable reuses of school wording, not a hidden technical definition.

Senses.Explanation: A warning that being held fast by verbal clauses leaves a person confused. It commonly completes the paired line that those who merely accept words are lost. Longxiang poses the inherited four-clause warning as a challenge to Zaian Xian. Gushan Yan and Tianru Weize use it in hall addresses before pressing beyond wording. Dahui Zonggao quotes the formula and asks about one who neither accepts words nor sticks to clauses; Yulin Tongxiu and Fushi repeat it in later addresses.

Senses.Explanation: Sitting upright (端坐) means holding the body erect while seated. Occurrences.Kwic: 舉。金牛行食次。問龐居士。生心受食淨名已呵。去此二途。居士還甘否。士云。當時善現豈不作家牛。云豈干他事。士云。食到口邊被人奪却。金牛便行食。士云。不消一句子。師拈云。善現作家金牛奇特。盡被龐居士一時領過了也。只如龐居士道不消一句子。且道。是那一句。端坐受供養。施主常安樂。

Occurrences.Kwic: 毗陵芙蓉太毓禪師一日，因行食到龐公前，公擬接，毓乃縮手曰：生心受食，淨名所呵。去此一機，居士還甘否？公曰：當時善現豈不作家？毓曰：非關他事。公曰：食到口邊，被人奪却。毓乃行食。公曰：不消一句。昭覺勤云：善現作家，芙蓉奇特，盡被龐老子一時領過了也。只如道不消一句，且道是那一句？端坐受供養，施主常安樂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1296.xml). Compilation of the School Gate’s “Raising Old Cases”. Speaker: Yuanwu Keqin.

Occurrences.Kwic: 示眾，舉：「龍牙云：『天下名山到因腳，辛苦年深與襪著，如今老大不能行，手裏把箇破木杓。』五祖演和尚云：『腳也不能著草鞋，手也不能把木杓，端坐受供養，施主常安樂。』」師云：「盡大地是一隻破艸鞋，盡大地是箇破木杓，要把便把，要著便著，佛祖何曾摸得著？」

Occurrences.Kwic: 曹居士請升座。「婺州信士曹仁卿，同合宅貴眷就寺設齋俵嚫，請老僧升座說法。老僧曰諾。會麼？盡大地是箇老僧，盡大地是箇法座，更教老僧升甚麼座？說甚麼法？記得五六年前行橋時，已曾到宅叨齋受嚫，今日山中三四百眾喫齋受嚫，人人歡歡喜喜。只者歡歡喜喜，增仁卿多少福田？長仁卿多少壽量？適來長老已為仁卿向法座上舉揚，老僧只喫齋受嚫便了，不用為蛇畫足，自然水到渠成。豈不見五祖演和尚云：『端坐受供養，施主常安樂。』趙州云：『老僧在者裡坐地，更說什麼佛法？』無明有條攀條，無條攀例？忽有箇漢出來道：『和尚！你坐地分贓，他日作箇什麼填還施主去？』只向道：『不作牛兮定作驢。』因甚如此？大丈夫異類中行，不是差事。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB273.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Qianyan. Speaker: Wuzu Fayan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南屏冬至，叢席荒凉，直是無可施設，賴有庫司都寺與堂中首座前日作那一場佛事不同，小小離四句、絕百非，攪酥酪醍醐為一味、鎔缾盤敘釧為一金，令我現前一眾、三世諸佛、歷代祖師、五百十六大阿羅漢均飽禪悅法喜，眼裏也飽、耳裏也飽，不覺手之舞之、足之蹈之，歡喜踴躍，向宗鏡光中同聲贊歎，云：希有，希有！奇哉，奇哉！於食等者，於法亦等；於法等者，於食亦等。山僧只管端坐受供養，且道與五祖相去多少？良久，云：其施汝者，不名福田；供養汝者，墮三惡道。

Occurrences.Kwic: 復舉：「丹霞問僧：『從什麼處來？』僧云：『山下來。』霞云：『喫飯也未？』僧云：『喫飯了。』霞云：『將飯與汝喫底人還具眼麼？』僧無語。後來長慶問保福：『將飯與人喫，報恩有分，因甚麼卻不具眼？』福云：『施者、受者，二俱瞎漢。』慶云：『盡其機來還成瞎不？』福云：『汝道我瞎得麼？』」師云：「丹霞、長慶、保福總合喫山僧手中棒，獨許者僧出一頭地。何故？不見道：端坐受供養，施主長安樂。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Speaker: Tian'an Sheng.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃云：「今此一會知識，施者、受者各各同具金剛正眼。施者若不具金剛正眼，如何來此選佛場中廣修供養？受者若不具金剛正眼，如何來此選佛場中端坐受供？所以道：端坐受供養，施主常安樂。卻笑淨名小家子，生心受施，種種呵責。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Speaker: Tian'an Sheng.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「世尊瞻前不顧後，雲門氣宇如王，惜乎棒頭短。金粟別無長處，每到四月八，只可殿裏燒香，大展坐具三拜，要伊端坐受供養，施主嘗安樂。」良久，云：「也是就貨還錢。」

Occurrences.Kwic: 身穿施主衣，口喫施主飯，將什麼報答施主？寺門西，田隴畔，負鞍戴角底豈是別人？束莖草置在面前，卻又吞吐不下，所以古者道：『入道不通理，還身復信施。』此之謂也。「有般漢聞與麼道，便云：『端坐受供養，施主常安樂。』似這等，別造地獄著汝在。更有云：『終日穿衣不曾掛寸縷絲，終朝喫飯不曾咬半粒米。』似這等，超果棒折亦未肯放過。

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃云：「昨夜三更，文殊、普賢起佛見、法見，各與二十拄杖，貶向二鐵圍山。敢問大眾：佛見、法見尚遭貶斥，世俗塵勞諸見還免此過麼？或有箇禪和子道：『百花叢裏過，一葉不沾身。』腳跟下早已泥深三尺。更道：『端坐受供養，施主常安樂。』生心受食，淨名早訶，直饒不見一法，猶有大過患在。

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日，侍老和尚次，尚問：「大脩行人未審得何果報？」師云：「拖犁拽耙。」尚云：「大造業人得何果報？」師云：「端坐受供養。」尚云：「爭奈以善為惡、以惡為善？」師云：「和尚自生分別。」尚云：「如何是汝不分別底？」師云：「合取口。」尚休去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB448.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lingji. Speaker: Lingji Xingguan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉：「昔石霜、山慶諸禪師在溈山為米頭，一日篩米次，溈曰：『施主！米莫拋撒。』霜曰：『不拋撒。』溈於地上拾得一粒，曰：『汝道不拋撒，這個是甚麼？』霜無對。溈又曰：『莫輕這一粒，百千粒盡從這一粒生。』霜曰：『百千粒從這一粒生，未審這一粒從甚麼處生？』溈呵呵大笑，歸方丈。至晚，上堂云：『大眾！米裏有虫也須好看。』」乃云：「只是一粒米，溈山老漢偏生大驚小怪，爭似龍舒眾善信五四年來倒廩傾倉供我一眾，實不止百千萬粒已也，天寧更不問他所從生，但只端坐受供養，自然施主獲安樂。然七百年來者道真言無人補闕今日山僧補闕去也。待溈山問：『汝道不拋撒，這一粒呢？』只向他道：『一點也瞞和尚不得。』至後，石霜復問：『百千萬粒從這一粒生，且道這一粒又從甚麼處生？』但叉手向前道：『也不較多。』只此兩語，擬質之八十行腳底老趙州，未審還為我一點首否？」良久，云：「放待冷來看。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. Speaker: Yushan Shangsi.

Occurrences.Kwic: 謝聖恩老和尚齋，上堂。舉：「昔演祖偈云：『山前一片閒田地，叉手叮嚀問祖翁，幾度賣來還自買，為憐松竹引清風。』沒量大人被片閒田地使得七上八落，雖引得些松竹清風，何能濟叢林實事？爭似我聖恩法叔自到祖翁地上，金鋤不動，靈苗自生，今以玉粒炊香餉我，一眾不信，但看缽裏飯、碗裏羹從何處得來？諸仁能下得口，不惟芬生齒頰，抑且甘潤咽喉，人人一飽忘饑，不異雪峰、鰲山成道時也。直饒金牛托出法堂底應難媲美，維摩擎來香積底未易較優，自非真慈注念、普行存心，何能有此盛作？爾諸大德有向食堂裏道得箇慶讚句，庶博山頭和尚熙怡一笑，不然端坐受供養，豈不慚惶殺人？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. Speaker: Yushan Shangsi.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB418.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huiyue Xu. Speaker: Huiyue Xu.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃舉：「金牛和尚每自做飯供養大眾，至齋時舁飯桶到僧堂前作舞曰：『菩薩子喫飯來。』遂撫掌大笑。後來長慶道：『大似因齋慶讚。』雪竇又道：『金牛不是好心。』」師云：「今日杯渡要問現前大眾，因齋慶讚即且置，那裏是金牛不好心處？若檢點得出，日日饅頭，朝朝做飯，時消萬兩黃金，達者豈為分外，不然喫水也須噎。」良久云：「既爾一眾吝辭，山僧秪得自道去也。」遂合掌云：「端坐受供養，施主長安樂。」下座。

Senses.Explanation: The formula (端坐受供養, sitting to receive offerings) is the front half of a couplet whose back half always rides with it (施主常安樂, the donors are at ease). Wuzu Fayan coins it in his own record as the close of a counter: Longya Judun's verse laments the famous mountains reached on foot, the broken wooden ladle still in hand; Wuzu answers as Baiyun — these feet can no longer wear straw sandals, these hands can no longer hold the ladle; I sit and receive offerings, and the donors are at ease. Yuanwu Keqin then makes the couplet the answer to the case's own question: Jinniu serves rice to Pang Yun, who takes the whole move with one remark too many — and which is that one sentence? Sit and receive offerings, the donors at ease. From the Song into the Qing the couplet walks the halls as the standing answer at every offering occasion — Huanchu Guangfo answers the how-shall-I-thank-you question with it alone; Yanxi Guangwen has no leisure for churning heaven and earth, he just sits and receives — until Baichi Xingyuan warns that fellows who merely quote it build themselves a separate hell. The root and the counters. Wuzu Fayan's couplet is born refusing: refusing Longya's verse of the wandering years — the sandal worn through, the ladle broken in hand — with the claim that the old walker can no longer walk, and that his sitting itself is the donors' ease. Qianyan Yuanzhang raises verse and counter together and turns them his own way: the whole earth is one broken sandal, the whole earth is one broken ladle — to hold when he will, to wear when he will; have Buddha or patriarch ever touched it?. And Muchen Daomin, five centuries later, raises the same pair as the East Mountain ancestor's words and reverses himself with shame: this mountain monk has walked every famous mountain to the sky's corner and is bound for no reason into an abbacy; the monastery gates falling in should be rebuilt — put the straw sandals back on, take up the ladle; is there then a way to repay the donors? Plow the green sea through and the harvest is sure; iron dumplings boil in the golden cauldron. The one sentence and its transmission. Yuanwu's turning-word works the Jinniu case line by line: asked whether mind-arising receipt of food holds, Pang calls back the food — one sentence too many; Pang took the whole exchange in one stroke, and the one sentence that settles it is the couplet. The Qing Raising Old Cases compilation transmits the same comment bound to the variant case in which it is Furong Taiyu who withdraws the ladle before Pang — one comment, two case-attachments, kept as the recension witness. And Xiaotang raises the other Jinniu case, the dancing rice-bucket: where exactly was Jinniu ill-intentioned? Answer that and every day is steamed bread; the assembly stays silent, so he answers himself, palms joined, with the couplet. The occasion answers. Asked how he will thank the donor for the meal, Huanchu Guangfo answers with the couplet alone, then draws a circle with his staff — do you see? do you hear?. Huiyue Xu, invited back to the ancestral seat and asked what blessing the donors' meal brings, gives the same whole-sentence answer. Yu'an Zhiji works it furthest: the stewards' work feeds monks and buddhas alike, equal in food, equal in the teaching — this mountain monk just sits and receives offerings, and how far is that from Wuzu? A long pause, then the reversal: what is given you is not called a field of blessing; those who feed you fall into the three evil destinies. The citations and the verdicts. Qianyan's alms address for the layman Cao recalls being fed at the same house years before, declines to preach over the meal, cites Wuzu's couplet, adds Zhaozhou's old I-just-sit-here — and answers his own challenge about repaying the donors with: not an ox, then an ass; a great man walking among other births is no disgrace. Tian'an Sheng rules on the raised rice-giving case: Danxia, Changqing and Baofu all deserve this monk's staff, only the unnamed questioner stands out — why? Is it not said. At the offering gathering he gives the ground: giver and receiver each carry the diamond eye, one to give widely, one to sit and receive — hence the saying; and then he laughs at Vimalakirti's small-mindedness in scolding mind-arising receipt. The police. Baichi Xingyuan, in the hall address that follows his winter furnace-opening, states the debt plainly: wearing donors' cloth, eating donors' rice, with what to repay them? The saddle-bearing, horn-wearing ox is nobody else; entering the way without understanding the principle, you repay with your very body. And there are fellows who hear this and just say the couplet — for the like of you they build a separate hell. Yikui Yuankui drives the same road deeper: should some chan monk claim to pass through a hundred flowers with not a leaf sticking, the mud is already three feet deep at his heels — and then go on to say the couplet: mind-arising receipt of food Vimalakirti long ago scolded; even seeing not one thing, a great fault remains. The bends. Lingji Xingguan, attendant to the old master, is asked what reward awaits the great practitioner: dragging plows and harrows. And the great karma-maker? Sitting and receiving offerings. The elder's why-call-evil-good is turned back on him — the old master generates the distinctions himself. Yushan Shangsi raises the Guishan rice-grain case — one grain dropped, and Guishan makes a fuss — and will not ask where the grain was born: he just sits and receives, and the donors win ease; then he patches the seven-hundred-year-old case with answers of his own and asks old Zhaozhou for a nod. At the thanks-address he sets the challenge: if one of you can utter a praising line in the dining hall, the old man on the hill will smile — otherwise, sitting and receiving offerings, would it not kill you with shame. And Baichi, on the Buddha's birthday, gives the couplet a third person: every fourth month he will just burn incense and bow with full mats spread — let HIM sit and receive offerings, the donors at ease; then, after a pause: still paying cash for the goods.

Senses.Explanation: Starving beside the rice basket is deprivation in immediate reach of food: the basket is present, yet the person remains unfed. Chan masters pair it with dying of thirst in the sea, apply it after Zhe’an Fan’s interlocutor misses a snowball held out before him, and use it to warn against overlooking what is plainly at hand. Yongji Rong’s verse names the impossible predicament of its Zen monk starving beside the rice basket. Sanshan Lai glosses Yunmen’s “rice in the bowl, water in the bucket” by warning not to starve beside the basket or thirst in the sea. Zhe’an Fan gives his interlocutor a ball of snow; when that interlocutor hesitates, Zhe’an says that those who starve beside the rice basket are numberless.
